en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Bīlíng during the Táng Dynasty.
First, in explaining the *Zhèngguān*, the intention for its composition is clarified; this is also termed "concluding the preceding and generating the subsequent.

Within this, there is first a brief explanation and then a detailed one. The initial passage concludes the preceding section, while the phrase "now, based on [the following]" generates the subsequent section. Question:
Within the first five summaries, there is both practice and understanding, as well as cause and fruit.
Why, then, is it said that only the six stages constitute understanding? Answer:
Regarding the "General Meaning" (Dà-yì):
it is placed at the head of practice and realization, as well as the causes and effects for oneself and others.
Since the underlying intent is difficult to manifest clearly, it is further explained through the categories of practice, realization, cause, effect, and so forth.
This does not mean that the fruits of practice and so forth already exist;
therefore, the general meaning is the totality,
while the remaining eight are the particulars.
This is a separate explanation of the causes and effects of practice and understanding,
similar to the beginning of the ten chapters in the explanation of the Dhyāna-pāramitā;
it is also the general purport.
The same applies to the general and specific meanings of "intention" (*manas*).
Furthermore, if there are those who, relying on the five preceding summaries,
practice to realize the fruit and are able to benefit others, this constitutes one path.
This is as recorded at the beginning of the third fascicle.
If the intent of the treatise pertains solely to the exegesis (*vyākhyāna*),
I fear that within such an exegesis, the explanation may not be exhaustive.
Therefore, one must thoroughly clarify the names, essences, and the inclusion of dharmas;
only then can the ten objects and ten vehicles that follow be established.
Although the *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states that there are ten different types of generating the bodhicitta, [it does not detail their specific characteristics].
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions between the four samādhis and the practice of clarity (*vidyā-caryā*),
merely listing their headings and defining their characteristics is insufficient;
therefore, [this text] has not yet touched upon the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) and the ten contemplations (*daśa-vipaśyanā*).
The skillful means (upāya), when compared to the five [stages], somewhat resemble the beginning of practice;
however, when compared to right contemplation (samyag-darśana), they do not yet constitute practice at all.
Furthermore, one sequentially traverses the twenty-five dharmas to generate understanding based on phenomena.
Only then can one be fit for the skillful means of authentic cultivation.
Therefore, the preceding six stages all belong to the category of understanding (*adhimukti*);
because they are established in reliance upon the teachings, they are said to be "based on the sūtras" (*sūtrāśrita*).
To distinguish it from partial and coarse understandings, it is called "sublime understanding.
Furthermore, the teachings upon which it relies do not differentiate between the Great and Small Vehicles or the partial and perfect;
for they together collectively constitute a single, perfect understanding.
Furthermore, the term *sūtra* encompasses all three baskets (*piṭaka*),
as in the case of the *Dharmottara*.
This is because the root treatise itself is also called *sūtra*;
furthermore, among the twelve divisions [of the canon], it is not restricted to a single section,
as the general name *sūtra* applies throughout from beginning to end.
Therefore, the various treatises, Vinayas, Mahāyāna, and Hīnayāna texts cited previously collectively establish this sublime understanding;
thus, they are now collectively designated as "Sūtra."
Regarding the term "arising subsequently":
one must employ the various preceding explanations before being able to proceed.
This is like how, in the explanation of names, one first awaits [the conditions] and only then severs [them].
The "Ultimate" (jue) merely opens up and clarifies the assembly of virtues, where differences together constitute the meaning of the ultimate.
The four sections revealing the essence all proceed from the partial to the perfect, thereby establishing the relationship between the relative and the ultimate.
The essence (tattva) is that which is explained;
since the name has been revealed, the essence follows the name.
The essence thus revealed universally encompasses all phenomena.
The characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are difficult to clarify; they are further divided into six meanings.
These apply universally to phenomena and principle, cause and effect, and self and other, each of which equally encompasses both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Furthermore, these are mutually encompassed through six principles;
then, by means of five gates, the phenomena they subsume are categorized.
Only then will one clearly understand how that which is subsumed within the essence of the body is mutually interfused.
Furthermore, having thoroughly understood that the provisional and the real are distinct yet harmoniously integrated without confusion,
one should further clarify them through the four chapters on the provisional and the real; thus,
one's perfect understanding will become somewhat more proficient.
Furthermore, one guides this understanding through skillful means;
when phenomena and principle are fused and unified, it is called "wondrous understanding.
Based on this wondrous understanding, one establishes correct practice.
If even such an understanding and practice that grasps the sublime principle is still difficult to master,
how much more so when one wishes to point specifically to a single passage within a particular section?
By what means can one ascend to the perfect, true, and wondrous stage?
One should know that this is because they have not yet perceived the principle of pervasive integration;
therefore, it is necessary to thoroughly understand the interlocking structure and the framing sequence of the preceding major chapters.
Gather and condense the essential meaning of the texts into a single mind;
furthermore, one must assemble the ten dharmas to form the vehicle,
harmonizing each element and scrutinizing every state of the objective realm.
Even assuming that those who have not yet awakened may serve as excellent causes for it—
just as when the Śrāvakas had attained the ultimate fruit,
they were rebuked by the Vaipulya sūtras and empowered by the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having come to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he requested three times and was refused four times;
yet it was still necessary for the five Buddhas to extensively and concisely reveal the provisional means,
with such earnestness and gravity through the causes, conditions, parables, and analogies.
There are still those who have not yet attained understanding and come to Nirvana;
how could it be that in the final age, those of dull faculties could secretly point to a single phrase and thereby discern the Buddha Vehicle?
It must necessarily accord with the subtle penetration of the phrases;
if it were not the six faculties, it would have to be the five grades.
Thus, the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Mind* says:
Those capable of answering such questions may be granted these five grades;
yet if one’s own mind already possesses such subtle mastery, why wait for external texts?
If you are still confused even while reading the text, I pray you do not presume to speak.
Therefore, the first six sections are all profound interpretations.
Thus, within each passage, the sequential and non-sequential [aspects], as well as the revelation of provisional means (*upāya*), are revealed in turn.
Only in the "Following One’s Own Intent" section is there a brief mention of the contemplation of the mind regarding the ten realms and the three truths.
The correct intention is simply to cultivate the sublime contemplation through the provisional and the real with a single mind;
therefore, it is said that "practice is established based on understanding.
This is explained in detail below, within the section clarifying the purpose of this passage.
First, the attainment of the person and the dharma is clarified.
Within this, the attainment through one's own practice is clarified first;
in each case, correct contemplation and sublime conduct are correlated with the sublime understanding of the preceding six chapters.
The first analogy illustrates how understanding and practice support one another.
The oil being able to sustain the light illustrates contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*);
the light being able to burn the oil illustrates contemplation and understanding (*vipaśyanā* and *adhimukti*).
The eye can lead the feet, which serves as an analogy for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
the feet can reach where the eye sees, which serves as an analogy for the practice of *śamatha*.
Both metaphors are presented together to illustrate these two dharmas.
"Phenomena" (xiàng) and "conditioning" (gèng), as well as "relying upon" (lài) and "depending on" (zī)—
though their ornate expressions differ, their underlying meanings must be mutually consistent.
"Lài" means to rely upon or depend on.
It provides benefit and support.
Therefore, one knows that without the practices of the preceding six chapters, cultivation cannot be perfected.
Regarding the "inferior causes" of practice and understanding, this explains how hindrances arise and clarifies the reasons why such hindrances arise.
Regarding the "three obstacles" and so forth:
these collectively bind the ten objects into three and four categories,
as explained in detail below in the section on the nine pairs and seven singles.
Because one observes the aggregates (*skandha*), various objects arise in mutual succession,
obstructing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and preventing them from being clear and tranquil.
In the text, for the sake of linguistic convenience, characters have been separated to form paired phrases.
This means that "heavy darkness and obscuration" refers to *vipaśyanā* (insight), while "vast distraction" refers to *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The character "heavy" (*chóng*) may be pronounced with either the level tone or the rising tone; both are acceptable.
"Dun" (sudden) follows the level; "mei" (obscure/depth) follows the profound. "Shenhou" (profound and deep) follows the superior.
"Ju" (great) means vast.
As for "da" (great), there is no dual sound; its meaning also applies to both.
When these [hindrances] arise frequently and are severe, they are termed "great.
This means that demonic obstacles (māra-antarāya) repeatedly appear, and each time they do so, they are profound and heavy.
Furthermore, because they are countered by their opposites, the term "demonic obstacles" is used as a designation for torpor and distraction (styāna-middha-vikṣepa).
Dullness and agitation are the obstructors;
heaviness and rigidity are the characteristics of the obstruction;
and obscuration and movement are the functions of the obstruction.
It is clear that these are the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although the habitual tendencies for concentration exist inherently, they remain faint;
because the beginningless habitual tendencies of the obstacles are powerful, the forces of dullness and agitation (*styāna-middha* and *auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) are predominant.
Regarding "the inconceivable," one contemplates the essential nature of demonic obstacles (*māra-vighna*).
If such obstacles arise, they will inevitably hinder contemplation and lead to rebirth in the evil realms;
therefore, one now intends to establish a contemplation so that these obstacles neither follow nor cause fear.
If one feels fear, it will invariably obstruct right practice;
if one follows along, one must still exercise discernment regarding what is progressive or regressive.
Should obstacles arise, they may all be drawn into evil.
Thus, they all head toward the evil realms (*durgati*).
Because their obstructions are not purely evil, they fall into the evil realms;
this is stated according to the majority of cases.
When the seven objects, such as the afflictions and illnesses, arise,
one falls into birth and death accordingly;
when the final two arise, one falls into the stage of skillful means.
However, the latter two objects exist within the initial state of mind,
and the former seven objects are fundamentally part of the cycle of transmigration;
both possess the quality of leading one into the evil realms.
Therefore, it is said that for the most part they belong to the process of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, one must distinguish whether the illness is neutral (avyākṛta) or gives rise to good or evil;
while afflictions invariably increase evil, [the illness] may not.
Among the karmas, the obscuring factors [kleshas] determine one's own good and evil;
Māra likewise causes people to fall into either good or evil.
Although dhyāna is a dull form of goodness, it is categorized as evil because it gives rise to slander.
Actions performed based on views may be either wholesome or unwholesome;
however, pride is invariably unwholesome.
Therefore, from the side of evil, it drags one down and causes one to fall into the evil realms.
If one is drawn toward the side of the wholesome, one falls into the wholesome.
However, if one examines good and evil from the perspective of ultimate principle (*yukti*),
then even the latter two objects are termed "evil."
How much more so for the preceding seven?
Therefore, in the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, within the chapter concerning Subhūti,
the three unconditioned states (asaṃskṛta) are disparaged as being the three evil realms (durgati).
Therefore, fearing the extremes is the same [in both cases],
yet such sameness obstructs correct cultivation.
Following the extremes differs [from following the Middle Way] because their meanings regarding the evil realms are distinct.
The following shall now clearly explain the establishment of the contemplation.
It is not by means of fear that one can reach Bodhi.
Although concentration and clarity, as well as dullness and distraction, are both inherently present in their essence, [one must cultivate the former].
The two [states] have no dual essence; their substance is one while their names differ.
Therefore, the names "dullness" and "distraction" lack any substantial reality;
they take stillness and illumination as their very nature.
Therefore, one should know that although the roots of dullness and distraction may be flourishing,
one must cultivate stillness and illumination to penetrate them.
To illuminate this essence of dullness, a single contemplation encompasses all three.
When the distracted is still, it is luminous;
this stillness of the distracted substance unifies the three types of cessation into one.
When the still is distracted, it is tranquil. Thus, the distracted is tranquil.
This constitutes the great outline of inconceivable *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, consisting of the nine objects such as stillness, illumination, illness, and so forth.
The following section, beginning with "like a pig," establishes a metaphor for initiating practice based on understanding.
This is like the preceding [analogy] for the calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) of tranquil illumination.
The first two analogies illustrate calming, while the latter two illustrate insight;
that is to say, as agitation and distraction increase, they all the more benefit the tranquility of calming.
When darkness increases and becomes more intense, one observes light all the more clearly.
According to the oral tradition of Juechen, this explains that "the pig rubs" is a metaphor for the understanding of *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The various streams are like the practice of tranquility (śamatha);
the blazing firewood is like the understanding of insight (vipaśyanā);
and the fanning wind is like the cultivation of insight.
At first glance, this seems acceptable, yet it still deviates from the intent of the text.
Previously, the analogy of "oil and light" was used to illustrate both understanding and practice;
here, however, it merely illustrates how practice is simultaneously obscured and dispersed, yet simultaneously illuminating and quiescent.
However, it is correct to interpret this as each of the two similes corresponding respectively to śamatha and vipaśyanā;
the simile of the pig rubbing itself [with dust] refers to the practitioner of śamatha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 30, in its commentary on the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), states:
"If a person inflicts evil upon one, it is like a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold;
the nature of the gold becomes even more pure. This is a metaphor for how, through patient endurance, the three obstacles and four māras are transformed and their stillness further increased."
Regarding "the various streams and so forth," as the Great Sūtra says:
"When the various streams enter the sea, they lose their original names;
though ten thousand currents all converge, their substance neither increases nor decreases."
The nine objects extend everywhere while the essence of stillness remains undiminished;
stillness is quiescent within movement, and movement increases the state of stillness.
Therefore, the surging current is used as a metaphor for movement.
Furthermore, the golden ocean is used as a metaphor for tranquility:
though the waves are numerous, the essence of gold remains unchanged;
though the currents flow in every direction, the nature of the sea does not increase.
The blazing of the fuel and so forth is like a practitioner whose fire becomes more intense as the fuel increases; once it is intense,
it does not discriminate among the fuel.
The demonic obstacles become increasingly manifest;
this manifestation does not select its objects.
The wind increasingly seeks the net.
In the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, within the section explaining the Buddha’s emission of light, it asks:
[From] the soles of the feet up to the uṣṇīṣa.
Each one emits sixty trillion rays of light;
these may still be counted,
yet even with these lights, they cannot fill the three thousandfold world system.
How much more so for the ten directions? Answer:
The light of the body is the source of all lights.
From its origin, it emits immeasurable rays of light;
like the *kālakūṭa* insect,
whose body is minute yet becomes large when it encounters the wind.
Even unto the point of being able to swallow and devour all things,
the light likewise increases limitlessly as it encounters those with the capacity for deliverance.
It is just like this now:
while the power of contemplation has not yet been perfected and its illumination is not yet fully developed,
once it encounters an object and achieves illumination, its function becomes increasingly clear.
Because all phenomena arise, Prajñā arises;
even unto that which is neither arising nor non-arising,
the terms "borrower" and "loan" are used as metaphors for the subject and the object.
One contemplates darkness;
darkness increases when light is present.
Therefore, firewood and wind are used as metaphors for darkness.
Furthermore, the fire of the insects is used as an analogy for light;
thus, while the fuel is merely abundant, the characteristics of the fire become increasingly intense,
and while the wind is merely fierce, the bodies of the insects grow ever larger.
This section on the "Vajra Below" explains the mutual benefit achieved through the perfection of contemplation.
In the initial passage, the analogy first illustrates the profound depth of the merit of practice and understanding.
The phrase "vajra and so forth" praises the profundity of the merit of understanding.
"Stopping and contemplation (śamatha-vipaśyanā) resolve and dismantle the three delusions;
their firmness and strength praise the far-reaching virtue of practice.
Through the accumulation of the practices of stopping and contemplation, one transcends the wilderness of the two deaths."
The "Ganshan Fu" (Sweet Springs Rhapsody) in the *Wenxuan* states:
"Behold the refined strength of the Way and its Virtue.
Here, "strength" (*gang*) refers to the internal firmness of metal and stone.
"Array" (chen) refers to the deployment [of troops]. It means to arrange them in formation.
Among the *Liùtão* (Six Tactics) of the Duke of Tàigōng, there are arrays such as Heaven, Earth, Man, Clouds, and Birds.
Now, the Vajra Contemplation has no battle it cannot break;
since the three delusions are simultaneously crushed,
it is as if the five armies have all been defeated.
The area outside the outer city walls is called the *jiao* (suburb). The area outside the *jiao* is called the *ye* (wilderness).
The outer wall is three hundred *zhang* in height.
The outskirts are like four hundred;
the wilds are like five hundred.
Thus, breaking through the two deaths exceeds five hundred.
This is called "Crossing the Mountains.
Although one has not yet reached the ultimate state upon entering the first stage of practice,
one nonetheless uses the middle path to shatter the two types of death associated with the provisional means of the shared realm.
Although the principle is without differentiation, realization depends upon the fulfillment of practice to attain the name "Vajra," which is able to sever the three delusions;
and practice depends upon the advancement of realization.
It is called "firm and strong" because it is able to transcend the two deaths;
furthermore, as it relies on various phenomena, its names are not uniform.
Although the texts each speak of it separately, their meanings are in fact mutually supportive.
The section "Purity of Wisdom" below clarifies the aspect of mutual support between wisdom and practice.
"Wisdom" refers to the understanding of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; "practice" refers to the cultivation of the conduct of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
When practice is attained through understanding, practice becomes free from delusion;
when understanding is attained through practice, understanding achieves its fruition.
Thus it is said: "Wisdom purifies practice, and practice advances wisdom."
To illustrate how these factors support one another, four further analogies are presented:
illumination is like the sun’s light, and moisture is like rain.
When illumination and moisture are balanced, all things can flourish.
When practice and understanding are free from partiality, all virtues can be fully prepared.
Understanding is like a merchant leader, while practice is like the merchants themselves;
with both a leader and those who reach their destination, the place of jewels can be expected.
When practice and understanding are fully perfected, the true reality (*dharmatā*) is not far off.
When understanding purifies practice, practice becomes flawless; this is like polishing a gem.
When practice adorns understanding, understanding becomes delightful; this is like embellishing it.
Because they mutually support one another, they are said to be "interlaced.
In the section on "the single essence," the subsequent analogies are used to illustrate the three preceding analogies;
although they are described as mutually adorning one another, they are non-dual yet dual.
Fearing that practice and understanding might be suspected of being like illumination and moisture,
which remain distinct entities,
one discusses practice and understanding in terms of the single reality.
Mutually guiding one another, they reveal the reality itself:
just as two hands in essence are but a single body— non-dual yet dual—
they are able to purify that essence so that it is dual yet non-dual.
This does not merely clarify the attainment of transforming others;
since the sublime practices have been fulfilled, one gives rise to teachings to benefit others.
Therefore, it is said that it is not merely one's own practice alone.
This refers to the stage of the first abiding (*prathamābhūmi*).
Furthermore, "mastering the lower" refers to the initiation of the teaching;
it signifies expansion.
"Great. "Obstructing" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the act of stopping or hindering, such as the four māras.
"Impeding" (*nivaraṇa*) refers to the act of blocking or obstructing, such as the three obstacles (*trīṇy āvaraṇāni*).
The "three" and "four" are both real and fully possessed as explained below.
"Qi" (啟) means to open or reveal.
This refers to the stage where those of inferior capacity emerge from the true [nature] into the provisional [manifestation].
The middle and superior [levels] are not like those in the sixth fascicle.
Regarding "the artisan and so forth":
an artisan is one who produces objects.
He is a master craftsman of the vessel. He clearly understands that the merit for himself and others is accomplished [thereby].
If his practice and understanding are not comprehensive, both he and others will fail.
Therefore, the Great Master wrote in a letter to Jizang:
"If one has understanding but lacks practice, one cannot subdue others;
if one has practice but lacks understanding, one is deficient externally in transforming others."
The phrase "teachers of men" and so forth is an expression of praise.
One who is fully endowed with both practice and realization is capable of being a teacher to others;
such a person is a treasure of the nation.
After the death of Emperor Ling of the Later Han,
during the reign of Emperor Xian, there was Mouzi, who deeply believed in the Buddhist school.
He criticized and rejected the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi, composing a treatise in three volumes and thirty-seven chapters.
In the twenty-first section, "Rescuing the Śramaṇas:
Discussing Right and Wrong," a question is posed as follows: Laozi said:
"The one who knows does not speak; the one who speaks does not know.
It is further said:
"Great eloquence appears like stammering."
It is further said:
"The gentleman feels shame when his words exceed his actions.
If śramaṇas know the ultimate Way, why do they not sit and practice it?"
To engage in empty talk regarding right and wrong,
or distorted arguments concerning what is crooked and straight— is this not indeed a thief of virtuous conduct? Answer:
The Master also had something to say.
Had he not spoken, what would I have had to relate?
It is improper to know and yet remain silent.
One who neither knows nor speaks is a fool.
One who can speak but cannot act is a teacher of the state.
One who can act but cannot speak is a servant of the state.
Those who can both act and speak are the treasures of the state;
within the three ranks, only those who neither can speak nor can act are the thieves of the state.
Now it is said that he is a master who masters others;
therefore, he is called a "National Treasure. Mouzi also says:
One who carries gold does not display it to others;
who would know that there is a wondrous treasure within?
One who wears brocade does not go out of their door.
Who knows that within there lies hidden brilliance?
When a horse lies prostrate at its stall and refuses to eat, it is indistinguishable from the team of common, inferior steeds.
When a scholar harbors his voice and does not speak, he is no different from the ignorant.
The common scholars of today lack the intelligence of the eminent and talented;
yet they wish to dispense with eloquence,
failing to persuade even a single person while imagining themselves to possess great rhetorical skill.
For those of such a kind who sit and expect to attain the Way—
it is like one without eyes wishing to see or one without ears wishing to hear;
is this not difficult?
Therefore, now that your own practice is perfected, you must benefit others through teaching.
One who is capable of both expounding and practicing is worthy of being a national treasure,
as occurred during the twenty-fourth year of King Wei of Qi in the Spring and Autumn period.
The King of Wei asked the King of Qi, saying, "Does Your Majesty possess any treasures?
He replied,
"I have none."
The King of Wei said,
"Although my state is small, I possess ten pearls, each a foot in diameter,
which can illuminate twelve chariots ahead and twelve behind."
"Why is it that a state of ten thousand chariots has no treasure?
King Wei said, "The treasures I speak of are different from those of a king."
If one has ministers such as Tanzi and others,
each guarding a single corner [of the state], then states such as Chu, Zhao, and Yan will not dare to advance rashly;
if one guards against bandits and thieves, then travelers will not even pick up what they drop on the road.
"If one uses this as a general, they can illuminate a thousand li;
how could it be merely for twelve chariots?
King Wei departed feeling ashamed.
This is precisely the national treasure that is both capable of teaching and capable of practicing.
Furthermore, the following section correctly clarifies the giving of the Buddha-vehicle,
which is the mind capable of transformation.
Question:
Those who study the Perfect and Sudden Teaching have fundamentally practiced the unconditioned (wu-yuan).
How can it be said that they only begin to "study the Buddha" upon reaching the first stage (prathamā-bhūmi)?
Answer: To aspire to the ultimate state is what is meant by "studying the Buddha.
Furthermore, one should exert oneself so that those below and those in the middle act as they speak.
The Tathāgata likewise benefits others by means of that which he has realized;
therefore, he exhorts them to realize it for their own benefit.
This is the subsequent analogy.
If one employs provisional teachings to transform others, although the Dharma-gate may open, it is not called "emptying the treasury.
Now, within the single mind, the gate for benefiting beings is opened;
the secret treasury is emptied to reveal the true jewel.
Since the mind is inexhaustible, the treasury is also immeasurable;
since the treasury is immeasurable, the jewels are boundless.
Because it contains all phenomena, it is called a "treasury."
The essence of principle is without deficiency, which is illustrated by the analogy of a pearl;
this reveals that sentient beings possess an inherently existing treasury of awakening,
which does not come from elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "this jewel and so forth":
next, he again employs a metaphor to praise its essence and function.
First, he praises its essence by referring generally to the jewel.
Next, the function is praised by means of specific analogies.
Regarding the initial passage: this jewel may be compared to the interior of the wondrous essence, wherein all aspects of practice, understanding, cause, and fruit are fully present.
The emission of light is a metaphor for wisdom;
the raining of jewels is a metaphor for meditative concentration.
Wisdom is precisely the virtue of knowledge.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is itself the virtue of abandonment; it is the very essence of concentration and wisdom.
These two virtues constitute the two virtues of benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
Wisdom is self-benefit;
severance is benefit for others.
These two—self and other—are non-dual.
One explains these three virtues to others.
Now, the praise for what has been explained refers to "this jewel" and so forth.
The phrase "illuminating the darkness" and so on praises its function.
To speak of "illuminating the darkness" refers to the power of light;
it shatters the darkness of others' ignorance.
To speak of "abundance or scarcity" refers to the power of rain.
It enriches those who lack the wealth of the Dharma.
"Bright night" is a further explanation of illuminating darkness;
"relieving the destitute" is a further explanation of enriching the impoverished.
The phrase "arising sequentially from one another" below explains that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are mutually identical.

The phrase "the destruction of delusions and the perfection of merit and virtue occur simultaneously" means that the two wheels [of concentration and wisdom] advance together. The phrase "the completion of practice and the arrival at the ultimate" serves as a metaphor for this.
The two wheels traveling far represent the horizontal pervasiveness of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);
the two wings soaring high represent the vertical culmination of meditative concentration and wisdom.
"To soar" means to fly by flapping one's wings.
Therefore, the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains was tested by Śakra to see whether he was capable of bearing the heavy burden of bodhi;
for as a chariot can transport loads only when it has two wheels, so too must one possess both wheels to succeed.
A bird has two wings that enable it to fly upward;
yet, though one sees its possession of these wings, one does not yet know whether the person possesses profound wisdom.
In the sutras, this is fundamentally illustrated by the metaphor of the vehicle and the precepts being fully complete.
Now, this is used as a metaphor for the simultaneity of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Phrases such as "the luster of jade" serve as metaphors for the external manifestation of the perfected power of the practices of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The "luster of jade" represents the virtue of *śamatha*, while the "vivid brilliance of emerald" represents the virtue of *vipaśyanā*.
